name: Groovy
title: Groovy (5.x)

type.text: **Dynamic typing is the default**: A `def` declaration defers method resolution to the runtime metaclass protocol, so a mismatch is reported when the line runs rather than when the file compiles (T1, T3)
**`@CompileStatic` and `@TypeChecked` restore compile-time checking**: Groovy 2 and later can compile a class to direct bytecode, and the annotated class is checked in the manner of Java
**Generics are erased on the JVM**: `List<String>` is a `List` at runtime, so a cast or a reflection call can reach a type the declaration does not admit
**Traits compose behaviour without inheritance**: A `trait` may carry default methods and state, so behaviour is mixed in rather than inherited from a superclass
**Safe navigation separates the test from the call**: `a?.b` short-circuits to `null` at the point of use, so the absence test stands where the value is read
**Operator overloading is by method name**: `a + b` may call `plus` and `a[i]` may call `getAt`, so a dense expression can invoke user code the syntax does not show

construction.text: **Mutability is the default**: A field is mutable unless it is `final` or the class is annotated `@Immutable`
**GroovyBeans generate the accessors**: A property declaration is compiled with its getter and setter, so the boilerplate leaves the source
**Map constructors separate the arguments from their order**: `new Point(x: 1, y: 2)` names each value at the call site, so the call does not depend on positional order
**`@Immutable` makes a value type in one annotation**: It generates the tuple constructor, `equals`, `hashCode`, and a defensive copy of the fields
**AST transformations decide the shape at compile time**: `@Canonical`, `@TupleConstructor`, and `@Builder` generate constructors whose signatures are not written in the source

memory.text: **The JVM owns deallocation**: There is no free operation, and a collection is scheduled outside the program's control
**No RAII**: `@Cleanup` and `withCloseable` release a resource at the end of a declared block, but nothing runs automatically at the end of an arbitrary scope
**No ownership model**: A reference may alias or be shared freely, and the collector decides when the object dies
**`withCloseable` binds release to a closure**: `stream.withCloseable { ... }` closes the resource when the block returns, including on an exception
**`@Cleanup` names the release point**: A local annotated `@Cleanup` is closed at the end of its enclosing block
**Collection is invisible in the source**: An allocation is a `new`, and no deallocation call is ever written

error.text: **Exceptions are unchecked**: Groovy requires no `throws` clause and the compiler does not check that a handler exists, so an exception may propagate from any call
**`try`/`catch`/`finally` is the structured path**: A `catch` clause names the type it handles, and `finally` runs on every exit
**`@TypeChecked` turns a type error into a compile error**: A call to a method that does not exist fails the build rather than the run
**Dynamic dispatch failure is a runtime exception**: A missing method or property raises `MissingMethodException` or `MissingPropertyException` at the call
**`?.` and `?:` suppress a failure by design**: Safe navigation returns `null` where an exception would otherwise report the fault

concurrency.text: **The JDK concurrency library is available**: `Thread`, `synchronized`, `java.util.concurrent` executors, and atomics are reached directly
**`@Synchronized` puts the monitor on the declaration**: The annotation transformation wraps a method in the object's monitor, so the lock is stated beside the method
**GPars adds dataflow, actors, and parallel collections**: The abstractions are a library over the JDK, so a concurrent design is not limited to threads and locks
**Shared mutable state is the default**: A field is reachable by every thread, and the compiler checks no access pattern
**No structured concurrency in the language**: A task tree, a scope, and a join are the JDK executor's responsibility, and Groovy adds no scope construct of its own

platform.text: **Runs on the JVM and interoperates with Java**: Any Java class is callable, and most valid Java is valid Groovy
**Compiles to standard JVM bytecode**: The output is a class file, so any JVM accepts it and the JDK's tools apply
**The JVM is the only target**: There is no non-JVM implementation of Groovy, so a program couples to one runtime
**Gradle and Jenkins Pipeline give it a first-class host**: The build and CI systems execute Groovy directly, which is why the language is present in most Java builds
**`@Grab` resolves a dependency from the script**: The annotation fetches an artifact from a repository at compile time, so a script couples to a repository and a version

performance.text: **`@CompileStatic` approaches Java**: The annotation emits direct bytecode calls, so the dynamic dispatch cost is removed for the annotated class
**The JVM JIT optimises a hot path**: The HotSpot compiler applies its full pipeline to the generated bytecode
**Collection pauses are inherited from the JVM heap**: A stop-the-world or concurrent cycle is scheduled by the collector the program chooses, not by the program
**Dynamic dispatch costs in dynamic mode**: A call site without `@CompileStatic` goes through the metaclass protocol, so the per-call overhead is higher than Java's
**JIT warm-up precedes peak speed**: A short script or a test run finishes before the compiler has optimised the hot path

ecosystem.text: **Apache top-level project**: The language is governed by the ASF, so it is not owned by one vendor
**The whole Java library ecosystem is available**: Any Maven artifact is usable from Groovy, resolved by the ordinary Java build tools
**Gradle and Jenkins Pipeline are built on it**: The two most common build and CI systems make Groovy a mainstream presence
**Grails and Spock are established projects**: The web framework and the testing framework are mature and maintained
**Groovy-specific libraries are few**: Most dependencies are Java libraries, so a Groovy-only package is less likely to exist

evolution.text: **Apache governance with published release notes**: A change is recorded in the release notes and the language documentation
**Java source compatibility is maintained**: Most valid Java keeps compiling as Groovy
**Groovy 5.x improves performance and JDK support**: The 5.x line raises the runtime baseline to the modern JDK
**`@CompileStatic` can be adopted file by file**: A project migrates incrementally rather than all at once
**There is no fixed release cadence**: The timing of a release is the project's decision, so a needed fix has no promised date

domain.text: **Build automation is a primary domain**: Gradle's build scripts are Groovy, and the DSL reads as a configuration
**CI pipelines are a primary domain**: Jenkins Pipeline scripts are Groovy, in the `Jenkinsfile` form
**Web development is supported by Grails**: The framework carries the persistence, routing, and view layers
**Testing is supported by Spock**: The specification framework defines a given/when/then DSL in Groovy
**The host framework can own the architecture**: A Gradle build script and a Jenkins pipeline run inside the host's execution model and its conventions, so the code couples to that model
**Application code usually prefers Java or Kotlin**: Groovy's share of general JVM application work is smaller than its share of scripting and build work

learning.text: **Gentle for a Java developer**: Most valid Java is valid Groovy, so an existing file compiles
**Typing is optional**: A script can start with `def` and add `@CompileStatic` later
**The closure and builder idioms read like the domain**: `each`, `collect`, and the builder pattern remove loop and assembly boilerplate
**The dynamic model is a large corner**: The metaclass protocol, method-missing dispatch, `ExpandoMetaClass`, and the differences of `@CompileStatic` from Java must each be learned
**Two compilation modes are two languages**: Code that compiles under `@CompileStatic` is a subset of dynamic Groovy, so a developer must know which rules apply where

syntax.text: **Concise and Java-compatible**: A statement needs no semicolon, no type, and often no parentheses
**Properties replace explicit accessors**: `x` reads `getX()` and `x = v` calls `setX()`, so the accessor is not written
**GString interpolation is built in**: `"Hello $name"` embeds an expression in a string literal
**Optional `return` and statement-value rules shorten a method**: The last expression is the result
**Operator syntax invokes methods**: `a + b`, `a[i]`, and `a << b` may call `plus`, `getAt`, or `leftShift`, so the notation hides the call
**Parenthesis omission can be ambiguous**: `foo bar baz` depends on the method-call rules, which the reader must resolve

testing.text: **Spock is a first-class framework**: given/when/then blocks, data tables, and mocks are a Groovy DSL over JUnit
**JUnit works directly**: A plain JUnit test class is a Groovy class
**`assert` prints the intermediate values**: A power assertion reports each subexpression of a failed assertion, which localises the failure without a debugger
**Metaprogramming builds test doubles**: `ExpandoMetaClass` and map coercion can stub a method without a mocking library
**A dynamic failure appears only when the test runs the line**: For a `def` call path the test is the first check
**`@CompileStatic` changes what a test can patch**: A statically compiled class does not consult the metaclass, so a stub installed that way has no effect

security.text: **Memory safety is the JVM's responsibility**: A buffer overflow or a use-after-free is not expressible in Groovy code
**The JDK security stack is available**: TLS, the cryptography providers, and the access-control APIs are directly usable
**Metaprogramming can cause type confusion**: `ExpandoMetaClass`, `methodMissing`, and `invokeMethod` change dispatch at runtime, so a call may reach code the source does not name
**Script execution is a code-execution surface**: `GroovyShell`, `Eval`, and `evaluate` run arbitrary text, so untrusted input must never reach them
**An AST transformation executes at compile time**: A build-time transformation runs code in the build, which is a supply-chain surface
**`@Grab` pulls code into the build**: The resolved artifact is loaded onto the script's class path from a remote repository

tradeoffs: **Dynamic or static compilation is a per-file choice**: `@CompileStatic` buys speed and checks at the cost of the metaprogramming forms it cannot compile
**DSL-friendly syntax trades precision for brevity**: Optional parentheses and dots make a DSL read well and a fragment ambiguous
**`def` is a productivity trade**: Less typing now, a later failure at run time
**`ExpandoMetaClass` is a deliberate escape hatch**: It is a scope and architecture decision, and its hidden reach is the price of the flexibility
**Java source compatibility is a target**: Most valid Java remains valid Groovy, which constrains the syntax as much as it helps
**There is no fixed release cadence**: The release schedule is the project's own decision
verdict: Groovy's design yields moderate core coupling, and a platform cost driven by the JVM and its dynamic dispatch rather than by the syntax. `@CompileStatic` and `@TypeChecked` convert the dynamic default into a checked and fast one, traits compose behaviour without inheritance, and safe navigation puts the absence test at the point of use. Main strengths: the whole Java ecosystem is reachable, Gradle and Jenkins Pipeline give the language a mainstream host, and Spock makes testing first-class. Main weaknesses: `def` defers failure to run time, the JVM is the only target, exceptions are unchecked, the metaclass protocol can change dispatch invisibly, and no structured concurrency exists in the language.

energy.text: Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.
